name: GUAC-Y HORROR PICTURE SHOW BURGER (Smothered in guacamole)

recipe.history:
The avocado — Persea americana — is one of the oldest cultivated fruits in the Americas, with evidence of its consumption stretching back seven thousand years to the Tehuacan Valley in central Mexico. The Aztec word for avocado, ahuacatl, entered Spanish as 'aguacate' and eventually as 'avocado' in English. The Aztec civilization built elaborate guacamole preparations — the word itself derives from the Nahuatl ahuacamolli, meaning avocado sauce — combining mashed avocado with tomatoes, chili peppers, onion, and wild herbs. These preparations were not merely food but carried spiritual significance; the avocado was considered a symbol of fertility and abundance and was associated with the Aztec god Quetzalcoatl. Spanish conquistadors brought descriptions of guacamole back to Europe in the sixteenth century, but the avocado itself was difficult to transport and did not take root in European cuisine. It remained primarily a fruit of the Americas, central to Mexican, Central American, and eventually Californian food culture.

Guacamole's transformation from a regional Mexican preparation into an American cultural fixture happened gradually through the twentieth century, accelerating dramatically with the growth of Tex-Mex restaurant culture in the 1970s and 1980s and California cuisine's embrace of avocado in the same period. The avocado toast and guacamole obsession of the 2000s and 2010s brought the preparation to its current status as one of America's most consumed condiments. On a burger, guacamole functions as sauce, fat supplement, and vegetable topping simultaneously — it replaces or augments mayo, provides creaminess and acid from the lime, and brings the heat of jalapeño and the brightness of cilantro. The 'smothered in guacamole' preparation, where the guac is heaped generously over the entire patty rather than applied as a thin spread, is an act of commitment that the burger fully deserves.

The first truly great guacamole I ever made was an accident. I was following a recipe that called for one jalapeño and misread it as one poblano pepper. The result was much milder, but somehow creamier and more nuanced, with a gentler heat that let the avocado and lime speak for themselves. I put it on a burger that same day, piling it on with a soup spoon, and ate it standing at the counter. My partner walked in, looked at the amount of guacamole I had used, looked at me, and said nothing but reached over and put more on hers. That is the correct approach.

Medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is the mandatory temperature for a burger smothered in guacamole. The guacamole is cold or at room temperature, bright with lime acid, rich with avocado fat, and punctuated with the crunch of onion and tomato. It needs a patty that is warm, deeply savory, and fat-rich to balance it. A well-done patty has expelled its fat and juices; it is a dry disk under a mountain of green, and the whole thing tastes flat. A medium-rare patty is still carrying all its richness, and the warm beef fat mingles with the avocado fat in a way that is genuinely extraordinary. This is a burger that requires courage of conviction — cook it right, pile on the guac without restraint, and serve it immediately.
ingredients: 1 jalapeño, seeded and finely minced (or with seeds for more heat)
2 Roma tomatoes, seeded and finely diced
1/2 cup fresh cilantro leaves, roughly chopped
2 chipotle peppers in adobo, finely minced
instructions: 1. Make the telera-style rolls: Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water; bloom 10 minutes. Combine flour and salt. Add yeast mixture, warm milk, and lard or shortening. Mix with dough hook on medium 8 minutes until smooth and slightly soft.

2. Cover and rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 4 pieces. Shape into oval rolls about 5 inches long. Using a dowel or the handle of a wooden spoon, press two parallel indentations along the length of each roll to create the classic telera shape. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet; proof 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 18–20 minutes until golden. Cool.
3. Make the chipotle mayo: Combine all ingredients, stir well, season. Refrigerate.

4. Make the guacamole: Cut avocados in half, remove pits, and scoop flesh into a large bowl. Using a fork or potato masher, mash to a mostly smooth texture with some chunks remaining — do not over-process. Fold in jalapeño, white onion, garlic, diced tomatoes, cilantro, lime juice, salt, cumin, and cayenne. Taste and adjust lime and salt. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the guacamole and refrigerate until assembly. Make no more than 1 hour before serving for best color.

5. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into oval or round 3/4-inch-thick patties slightly wider than the buns. Press a center dimple. Season generously on both sides with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and cumin.
6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add oil.

7. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes until deeply caramelized and crusted. Flip once. Place a slice of pepper jack cheese on each. Cook 2–3 minutes more, tenting to melt cheese, until center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). Rest on a rack 3 minutes.
8. Split telera rolls and toast cut-side down in the skillet fat 60–90 seconds.
9. Assemble: Spread chipotle mayo on both cut faces of each roll. Place shredded iceberg on the bottom roll, followed by sliced tomato and white onion; season tomato with flaky salt.

10. Place the cheese-topped patty on top. Using a large spoon, smother the patty generously — enthusiastically — with guacamole. Do not be shy. The patty should be largely concealed under the guacamole.
11. Squeeze a little fresh lime juice over the guacamole. Cap with the top roll, press gently, and serve immediately with extra lime wedges.
